title: House Reed and the Birth-flower Shrine — Low Kiln, Sill
caption: The reed-cutter's house east of the Clay Yard, Alda Reed's dwelling, drawn close at the scale of a basket set just inside the finger's-width-open door: the one room with its hearth and slip pot, the bench by the door with a birth-slate propped writing-down, the board-bed whose grey wool holds a warmed stone at the belly, the grey Ash ridge left where it lies, bundles of cut reeds inside and at the threshold, and the loose board lifted at one end under which six narrow pages lie face-down in a second hand with no seventh written. A few paces east stands the birth-flower shrine, the hearth-maids' niche where the district's birth-slates lie overnight: five slates on the flat stone, a candle end of beeswax, a curl of grey wool, the slate-box of answered slates at its foot, and the crossed mark cut into the stone above, drawn and not explained. Around both, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the Drawing house, House Silt, the smithy, the drying racks, the slip pits and the yard well; the Slip Brook clay-heavy along the north, the Ilm below, the walk the women take from the house to the niche, and the Clay Road west to the Cross and east to Greybank, with the reedbeds going off toward Reedholt. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor's notes on the hand that goes to the slate before the child, the mark for which a priest gave a date and did not look up, the six pages no Court physician has seen, and the date laid over a sign that no living person can take off. An engraved bundle of cut reeds sits in the margin.
